shared_text:
The flight. An airliner arriving over mountainous terrain, in daylight and clear visual conditions.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying and the captain the pilot monitoring.

What happened. The crew were cleared on an arrival to join an RNP approach. They had briefed the terrain and had the terrain display on. About 35 miles out, air traffic control assigned a heading until 25 miles from a beacon and cleared them to 4,000 ft. Approaching 25 miles, ATC cleared them direct to the final approach fix and, a few seconds later, for the approach. A procedures note said not to accept a clearance direct to a fix unless it was outside the final approach fix; the captain understood this to apply only to approaches with curved legs. The crew armed the approach; the flight display showed the final approach mode and a vertical deviation indicator. About 20 miles out, they set 2,800 ft in the altitude window, then 4,000 ft for the missed approach as the aircraft captured the path, and followed it down. They did not refer to the minimum vectoring altitude chart. They could not see the airport, which they knew was beyond the mountains in view. Approaching about 3,100 ft, still well clear of terrain, both pilots agreed it did not look right and decided to climb to 4,000 ft. As they began climbing, ATC issued a climb to 3,300 ft. The crew asked for 4,000 ft and climbed until sure of terrain clearance.
safe_outcome: The crew then rejoined the approach, which was normal from that point. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was descending nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = descending; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Single narrative (captain, pilot monitoring). Rule 3, removed: the 'Cause' section's chart criticism and recommendations (10-7 notes, training, telling crews not to accept the fix), 'we should have gone to' the earlier fix, 'we should have' used the MVA chart, 'we were fortunate it was VFR', and the comparison with past events elsewhere. Kept from that section as facts of the time: the terrain briefing and terrain display, the captain's understanding that the direct-to note applied only to approaches with RF (curved) legs, that the fix was the final approach fix, and that the crew did not refer to the MVA chart. Rule 5, moved to the safe ending: rejoining the approach and the normal approach from there. Rule 6: arrival name, approach and runway designator, navaid and fix names removed; 'northwest' dropped. Judgement calls: aircraft type is not reported ('Commercial Fixed Wing'), so 'an airliner'. Not stated: the captain's later view that the path from that fix led below the MVA and surrounding terrain (kept out as part of the Cause argument; the ATC climb and the crew's climb carry the fact). Bracket 'descending': the aircraft climbed back towards the arrival altitude, where other arriving traffic would be descending.
